final_proof:
For a family of nonnegative real numbers \((a_i)_{i\in I}\), write
\[
\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup\left\{\sum_{i\in F}a_i:F\subseteq I\text{ finite}\right\}.
\]
Thus the Hilbert direct sum is
\[
H=\left\{x=(x_i)_{i\in I}:x_i\in H_i\text{ and }\sum_{i\in I}\lVert x_i\rVert_i^2<\infty\right\}.
\]
We first verify that its usual inner product is well defined. If \(x,y\in H\), then for every finite \(F\subseteq I\), the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality in each coordinate and then in the finite-dimensional scalar space give
\[
\sum_{i\in F}|\langle x_i,y_i\rangle_i|
\leq \sum_{i\in F}\lVert x_i\rVert_i\lVert y_i\rVert_i
\leq \left(\sum_{i\in F}\lVert x_i\rVert_i^2\right)^{1/2}
       \left(\sum_{i\in F}\lVert y_i\rVert_i^2\right)^{1/2}
\leq \lVert x\rVert\,\lVert y\rVert,
\]
where \(\lVert x\rVert^2:=\sum_{i\in I}\lVert x_i\rVert_i^2\). Hence \((\langle x_i,y_i\rangle_i)_{i\in I}\) is absolutely summable, so
\[
\langle x,y\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x_i,y_i\rangle_i
\]
is defined. Here an absolutely summable family has its sum defined as the limit of its finite partial sums, directed by inclusion. Such a limit exists because the tails of the absolute-value family are arbitrarily small: if its finite partial sums are bounded and \(\varepsilon>0\), choose a finite partial sum within \(\varepsilon\) of their supremum. This also shows directly that finite-partial-sum limits respect addition and scalar multiplication.

The set \(H\) is a vector space under coordinatewise operations: for example,
\[
\sum_{i\in I}\lVert x_i+y_i\rVert_i^2
\leq 2\sum_{i\in I}\lVert x_i\rVert_i^2+2\sum_{i\in I}\lVert y_i\rVert_i^2<\infty,
\]
and scalar multiplication is immediate. Passing the inner-product identities in each \(H_i\) through the finite-partial-sum limits proves sesquilinearity and conjugate symmetry of \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\). Moreover,
\[
\langle x,x\rangle=\sum_{i\in I}\lVert x_i\rVert_i^2=\lVert x\rVert^2\geq0,
\]
and equality implies \(\lVert x_i\rVert_i=0\) for every \(i\), hence \(x=0\). Thus this is an inner product on \(H\), inducing precisely the norm displayed above.

It remains to prove completeness. Let \((x^{(n)})_{n\geq1}\) be a Cauchy sequence in \(H\), with \(x^{(n)}=(x_i^{(n)})_{i\in I}\). For every \(i\in I\),
\[
\lVert x_i^{(n)}-x_i^{(m)}\rVert_i^2
\leq \sum_{j\in I}\lVert x_j^{(n)}-x_j^{(m)}\rVert_j^2
=\lVert x^{(n)}-x^{(m)}\rVert^2.
\]
Consequently \((x_i^{(n)})_n\) is Cauchy in the Hilbert space \(H_i\). Let \(x_i\in H_i\) be its limit, and put \(x=(x_i)_{i\in I}\).

Every Cauchy sequence is bounded, so there is \(M<\infty\) such that \(\lVert x^{(n)}\rVert\leq M\) for every \(n\). If \(F\subseteq I\) is finite, coordinatewise convergence and continuity of the norm yield
\[
\sum_{i\in F}\lVert x_i\rVert_i^2
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i\in F}\lVert x_i^{(n)}\rVert_i^2
\leq M^2.
\]
Taking the supremum over all finite \(F\) shows that \(\sum_{i\in I}\lVert x_i\rVert_i^2\leq M^2\), so \(x\in H\).

Finally, let \(\varepsilon>0\). Choose \(N\) so that
\[
\lVert x^{(n)}-x^{(m)}\rVert<\varepsilon/2
\qquad(n,m\geq N).
\]
Fix \(n\geq N\) and a finite \(F\subseteq I\). Letting \(m\to\infty\) in the finite sum gives
\[
\sum_{i\in F}\lVert x_i^{(n)}-x_i\rVert_i^2
=\lim_{m\to\infty}\sum_{i\in F}\lVert x_i^{(n)}-x_i^{(m)}\rVert_i^2
\leq (\varepsilon/2)^2.
\]
Taking the supremum over finite \(F\) yields \(\lVert x^{(n)}-x\rVert\leq\varepsilon/2<\varepsilon\). Therefore \(x^{(n)}\to x\) in \(H\). Every Cauchy sequence in \(H\) thus converges in \(H\), so \(H\) is a Hilbert space.
